title: The Attractional Era
subtitle: From a tent in Los Angeles to the megachurch's high noon. How American Christianity learned to produce a crowd, what the production did to the message, and the honest audit that ended the era's confidence.

sections.title: A Tent at Washington and Hill
sections.body:
The era did not begin in a cathedral. It began in a tent, pitched at the corner of Washington Boulevard and Hill Street in Los Angeles in the fall of 1949, a canvas hall the papers took to calling the Canvas Cathedral. The campaign was planned to run three weeks. A thirty-year-old evangelist from North Carolina named Billy Graham preached under that canvas night after night, calling a city of migrants and strivers to the cross, and for the first stretch the results looked like every other tent revival America had already learned to ignore. Then Stuart Hamblen, a hard-drinking radio cowboy with a show half the city knew, walked forward, and announced his conversion on the air, and the city began to listen.

What happened next has been told the same way for seventy-five years. William Randolph Hearst, the newspaper baron, sent his editors a two-word directive: "puff Graham." Graham always said he never met the man and never learned his reasons. But the papers obeyed, and the wire services followed the papers, and the national magazines followed the wires. The crowds swelled until the three weeks became eight. Jim Vaus, a wiretapper who worked for the mobster Mickey Cohen, professed faith in that tent. So did Louis Zamperini, the Olympic runner who had survived a Japanese prison camp. By the time the poles came down in November, a regional preacher had become a national figure, and the instrument of his becoming was mass publicity, which the church did not build and did not control.

We should say plainly what kind of men these were, because the era's critics forget it and the era's children need it. A year before Los Angeles, in a motel room in Modesto, Graham and his small team had drawn up a private covenant against the sins that had made evangelists a national joke. They would put the money under outside control. They would never be alone with a woman not their wife. They would refuse to attack local churches. And they would never inflate their numbers. Read that last item again. In 1948, before the crowds ever came, these men already knew that counting was where evangelists lied first. They were sincere, and the sincerity is the point, and it will remain the point for the whole sixty years this essay covers. The attractional era was not built by hucksters. It was built by believers who wanted the lost found and who discovered that the machinery of mass culture could fill a tent.

Within a year Graham had founded his own organization and a national radio program, and the crusade became a repeatable event: the stadium booked, the choir assembled, the counselors trained, the decision cards gathered and passed to local churches for follow-up. In 1957 he filled Madison Square Garden night after night for sixteen weeks. The method worked, and everyone watching learned the lesson underneath the lesson. A crowd could be produced. Publicity, celebrity, organization, and a gifted man with a microphone could gather more people to hear the gospel in one night than a faithful parish pastor would preach to in a lifetime. No one in the tent asked what the method would do to the message once the tent became the model. That question waited sixty years for an answer. This essay is the story of the answer arriving.

sections.title: Mission Leaves Home
sections.body:
The energy of postwar evangelicalism did not flow through the denominations. It flowed around them. Youth for Christ organized in 1945 out of the Saturday-night youth rallies that had sprung up in wartime cities, hired Graham as its first traveling evangelist, and announced itself with a slogan that promised a movement "geared to the times" and "anchored to the Rock." Read the slogan slowly, because the whole era is folded inside it. The Rock was fixed. The gearing was negotiable. From 1945 forward, American evangelicalism would treat the presentation of the faith as an engineering problem, to be solved afresh for every generation and every market.

The organizations multiplied with astonishing speed. Bill Bright founded Campus Crusade for Christ at UCLA in 1951 and in time compressed the gospel into a booklet, the Four Spiritual Laws, that a trained student could walk a stranger through in minutes; its first law announced that God loved you and offered "a wonderful plan for your life." The Navigators, begun by Dawson Trotman in the 1930s to disciple sailors, taught Scripture memory and one-on-one follow-up with a rigor most congregations never attempted. The National Association of Evangelicals had organized in 1942. Fuller Theological Seminary opened in Pasadena in 1947. Christianity Today began publishing in 1956, founded at Graham's urging with Carl F. H. Henry at the desk, to give the movement a mind. In 1972 Campus Crusade filled the Cotton Bowl in Dallas for a week of training and music that the press compared to a Christian Woodstock. None of this was cynical. Real students met Christ in dormitories because a stranger with a booklet was not ashamed of the gospel, and only a fool would sneer at that.

But notice what the structure was quietly teaching. Evangelism now belonged to the crusade organization. Youth belonged to the rally. Students belonged to the campus ministry, discipleship to the Navigators, the intellect to the magazine and the seminary. Each specialized agency did its one task better than the local congregation had been doing it, and together they trained two generations to think of the local church as one provider among many, the place you attended between the organizations that did the actual mission. The efficiency was real. What the efficiency traded away was older than efficiency: the assumption that the congregation itself, the ordinary assembly of the baptized gathered around word and table, was the body through which God intended to reach the world. I was formed by the unbundled world, trained on its materials, and I remain grateful for it, which is exactly why I am implicated in what it cost. A church can contract out its mission for only so long before it forgets the mission was ever its own.

sections.title: The Missionary Who Counted
sections.body:
The theory arrived from the mission field, and the theory deserves a fairer telling than it usually gets. Donald McGavran was born in India in 1897 to missionary parents and gave his working life to that country. The question that seized him was empirical. Why did some peoples receive the gospel in great movements while mission stations sat for generations with a school, a clinic, and a handful of converts? His answer, worked out in The Bridges of God in 1955 and expanded in Understanding Church Growth in 1970, was that the gospel travels along the webs of family and kinship that already bind a people together. Individuals extracted one by one into the mission compound were cut off from every relationship through which the faith might have spread. Whole peoples, moving together, kept the bridges intact.

From this came the principle that made him famous and then notorious: his observation that people prefer to become Christians without having to cross barriers of race, language, or class. State his case at full strength, because it had one. In India, asking a Hindu to follow Christ meant asking him to abandon caste, family, marriage, food, and name in a single step, and McGavran's charge was that most of that price had been set by missionaries, not by Christ. The gospel demanded repentance. The mission compound demanded cultural suicide. Let a people come to Christ inside their own language and kinship, he argued, and then let discipleship do its slow work of breaking down the walls between peoples, for he never denied that the walls must fall. He insisted, too, that a mission count its results. Sheep are countable, he liked to point out, and a shepherd who refuses to count his flock cannot honestly claim to be feeding it. Counting, for McGavran, was not vanity. It was accountability, and coming from a man who had watched mission agencies report decades of activity with nothing to show for it, the demand was a form of truth-telling. Fuller Seminary gave him a school in 1965, and church growth became a discipline, with journals, doctorates, and disciples.

Then the theory crossed the ocean, and the ocean changed it. In the 1970s and 1980s McGavran's students, C. Peter Wagner chief among them, translated a missionary's field observations into a domestic science for American congregations: demographic studies, receptivity ratings, target populations, growth seminars. And here the honest verdict must be said. In India the homogeneous unit was a barrier the missionary grieved and worked within. In America it became a market the strategist selected and served. The suburbs were already sorted by race and income, sorted by the interstate, the mortgage map, and three centuries of sin, and a church built to grow along those lines did not merely tolerate the sorting. It baptized it. Graham himself had personally taken down the ropes that segregated the seating at his Chattanooga crusade in 1953. The science that scaled his era strung the ropes back up one zip code at a time and called the result receptivity. Worship remained the most racially divided hour of the American week, and now there was a theory to explain why the division was efficient. McGavran's defenders insist he was misread, and they are half right; he wrote that the walls must fall. But a principle that requires that much footnoting in a fallen country will be used without the footnotes. We took a description of how sinners come to Christ and turned it into a blueprint for keeping the sinners comfortable.

sections.title: The Drive-In Church
sections.body:
In 1955 a young minister named Robert Schuller arrived in Orange County, California, with instructions to start a church and almost nothing to start it with. He rented the Orange Drive-In Theatre and preached on Sunday mornings from the roof of the snack bar while his wife, Arvella, played the organ and the congregation listened through the window-mounted speakers of their cars. It sounds like a joke, and it was a strategy. Southern California was filling with migrants who had left their churches two time zones behind, and Schuller reasoned that the way to reach them was to remove every barrier between the man in the driver's seat and the message: barriers of architecture, of dress, of expectation, of demand. He went door to door asking unchurched neighbors what they wanted in a church, and then he built what they described. It is hard to overstate how new that was. For nineteen centuries the church had assumed it knew what the gathered people needed. Schuller asked the scattered people what they wanted, and the difference between those two questions is the hinge of this entire era.

Take the measure of what he preached, because the era learned that from him too. Schuller was a disciple of Norman Vincent Peale, whose The Power of Positive Thinking had sold America a religion of confidence in 1952, and he named his own version possibility thinking: sermons scrubbed of guilt and judgment, engineered to send an anxious commuter back into Monday believing in himself. The formula built an empire. The Hour of Power went on the air in 1970 and became one of the most watched religious broadcasts in the country. The Crystal Cathedral, a sanctuary of glass and steel by the architect Philip Johnson, was dedicated in 1980, built transparent on purpose, so that the man wary of church could always see his way out. And in 1982 Schuller published Self-Esteem: The New Reformation, in which he proposed that the church reorient its message around human need and recast sin itself in terms of damaged self-esteem. Mark that carefully. The therapeutic gospel was not a drift nobody noticed. It was a program, written down, with a Reformation named after it.

Be fair to the man: he reached people no church was reaching, and some of them moved through those glass doors into a faith deeper than the one preached from the snack-bar roof. But a church built on the customer's stated needs is leased, not owned, and the lease came due. The customers aged. The encouragement they had come for became available in newer formats from fresher faces. In October 2010, the year this era closes, Crystal Cathedral Ministries filed for bankruptcy, and the building was sold to the Roman Catholic Diocese of Orange, which worships in it today under an older name and an older theology. The glass church outlived the message it was built to broadcast. Every pastor of my generation should stand in that nave once and do the arithmetic. The old warning holds: what you win them with is what you win them to, and what you win them to you must keep supplying, forever, or lose them to the next supplier.

sections.title: Unchurched Harry
sections.body:
In October 1975 a youth pastor in his early twenties named Bill Hybels held the first service of Willow Creek Community Church in a rented movie theater in Palatine, Illinois. Before launching, he and his team had gone door to door through the surrounding suburbs asking people who did not attend church why not, and the answers came back with the consistency of a diagnosis. Church always asks for money. Church is boring. Church is irrelevant to my life. Church makes me feel guilty. So they built a church shaped by the answers. The weekend service was designed not for believers but for a composite man the team named Unchurched Harry: suburban, intelligent, suspicious of religious performance, unwilling to sing words he did not mean. Harry could come, sit in the dark, stay anonymous, hear professional music and a drama sketch and a plain-spoken talk on a question he was actually asking, and leave without being cornered. The believers' own worship and deeper teaching moved to midweek. The weekend belonged to Harry.

Here is what the critics of the seeker movement, and I have been one, are obligated to say first. Willow Creek was built by evangelistic sincerity. Unchurched Harry was loved before he was marketed to. Those young leaders grieved over lost neighbors, and they had grown up watching churches demand that outsiders master the dress code, the dialect, and the hymnal before they could hear the gospel, and they refused to keep charging that toll. The church grew because unchurched people actually came, and unchurched people actually came because someone had finally taken their objections seriously, and among the crowds were real conversions that no honest observer can wave away. The campus at South Barrington rose in 1981. The Willow Creek Association formed in 1992 to teach the model, and member churches took it up across the continents. By the 1990s Willow was among the most studied congregations in the world, and the first thing the era's pastors learned from it was excellence, the conviction that a shoddy service dishonors God and insults the guest. I learned it too. I have never fully unlearned it, and I am not sure I should.

The most careful outside study the church ever received came from a researcher named G. A. Pritchard, who spent a year inside Willow's services and staff meetings and published Willow Creek Seeker Services in 1996. His conclusion, offered with the sympathy of a man who liked the people he studied, ran roughly this way: the sincerity was real, and the method was quietly reshaping the message. Study Harry closely enough, build the weekend around his questions, his attention span, his suspicion of demand, and Harry's categories become the frame. The God on offer bends toward the psychological, the practical, the immediately useful. What a church rehearses every weekend is what a church becomes. The stage grew more professional, the watching grew more comfortable, and a question began forming that the movement was not yet ready to ask out loud. Willow had proved that a church could become excellent at gathering. Excellent at what else, nobody yet knew. The answer, when it finally came, would come from Willow itself, and it is waiting at the end of this essay.

sections.title: Purpose, Process, and the Corner Office
sections.body:
Rick Warren started Saddleback Church in southern California with an Easter service in a rented high school theater in 1980, having first walked his new neighborhoods with a notebook, asking the unchurched what kept them away. In 1995 he wrote the era's operating manual. The Purpose Driven Church deserves its due, because Warren saw the crowd problem clearly and said so in print. He drew the church as concentric circles, community, crowd, congregation, committed, core, and insisted that the whole point was movement inward. The crowd was raw material, not the finished product. A church that gathered a crowd and stopped had not yet done anything. Say it plainly: the era's best minds knew a crowd was not a church, and the system, the classes, the covenants, the process, was built to move people from the parking lot toward the core. In 2002 Warren opened The Purpose Driven Life with a sentence, "It's not about you," that cut straight against the current his own era floated on, and the book became one of the best-selling volumes in the history of American publishing. The era contained its own correctives. It stacked them at the front of every bookstore in America. That is what makes the final audit so sobering, and we are almost there.

But watch what the pastor was becoming while the system ran. Peter Drucker, the father of modern management, took a late-career interest in the American megachurch and regarded the large pastoral congregation as among the most significant social phenomena of his era; his admirer Bob Buford founded Leadership Network in 1984 to connect the biggest churches to the best management thinking; and from 1995 Willow Creek's Global Leadership Summit put executives, generals, and consultants on stage before auditoriums of church staff. The pastor's bookshelf migrated from theology to management. Churches acquired mission statements, org charts, brand consultants, and capital campaigns run by specialist firms. Be fair here as well. A congregation the size of a town must be administered, and Scripture itself shows Moses in the wilderness accepting a sensible piece of management consulting from his father-in-law. The drift was not that pastors learned administration. The drift was that the chief executive stopped being a metaphor. A CEO exists to grow the enterprise. His instrument panel is numerical. And what fills the instrument panel, attendance, giving, campuses, decisions, quietly becomes what fills the prayers.

Os Guinness saw it coming and said so in 1993, in a small book with a blunt title, Dining with the Devil, borrowed from the old proverb that a man who dines with the devil had better bring a long spoon. His warning, compressed: the church growth movement was borrowing the tools of the modern world, marketing, management, psychology, polling, without examining the assumptions carried inside the tools, and tools are never neutral. Use them undiscerned and the audience becomes sovereign, the method becomes the message, and the church wins the world on terms that turn out to be the world's. Almost no one stopped to argue with him. The rooms were filling, and nothing recruits like results. We brought a short spoon.

sections.title: The Soundtrack and the Broadcast
sections.body:
Every awakening writes its own music. The Wesleys gave revival its hymns; the Jesus People, the converted hippies who filled Chuck Smith's Calvary Chapel in Costa Mesa at the end of the 1960s and were baptized by the hundreds in the Pacific surf, gave it guitars. Maranatha Music formed in 1971 to carry their songs beyond the beach, and for a while the music was exactly what it appeared to be, new believers singing to God in the only musical language they had. Then the industry arrived. Through the 1970s and 1980s contemporary Christian music acquired labels, charts, radio formats, festivals, and stars, and by the early 1980s Amy Grant was crossing onto the mainstream pop charts. In 1988 a licensing clearinghouse, CCLI, organized the royalty stream for congregational song. Note what that means. From 1988 forward, the songs a church sang on Sunday morning were also a tracked and ranked market, and a worship song could hold a chart position before it had ever really been a prayer.

The full form arrived from Sydney. Brian and Bobbie Houston founded Hills Christian Life Centre in 1983; in 1993 its worship leader, Darlene Zschech, wrote Shout to the Lord, and the song traveled to congregations on every continent; and by the turn of the millennium the church had taken the name of its music brand and become Hillsong. Sit with that sequence. A congregation became famous for its recordings and then renamed itself after its product. The stage that Willow had professionalized was now lit, mixed, and directed to the standard of an arena tour, and the congregation completed its long migration into an audience: hands raised toward a platform, faces lit by a screen, the set list engineered for emotional arc, the songs written, tested, and released the way singles are released, because that is what they were. None of this required insincerity from anyone on the platform, and much of it was written in earnest to the glory of God. The structural fact remains. When the music must travel, the theology packs light, and a church that sings another church's charting products every week is being catechized by a market.

Meanwhile the era's broadcast wing preached a harder doctrine under brighter lights. The historian Kate Bowler, in Blessed, traced the American prosperity gospel to a braid of Pentecostal healing revival, the mind-power metaphysics of New Thought, and the national creed of upward mobility: a faith that reads divine favor in health and wealth. Oral Roberts carried the healing tent onto television in the mid-1950s, opened his university in Tulsa in 1965, and taught givers to plant what he called seed faith, money sown in expectation of return. Kenneth Hagin's Word of Faith movement systematized the confidence: name the blessing, claim the blessing. The televised empires rose through the 1980s, and in 1987 and 1988 the most visible of them fell in public, one broadcaster resigning in scandal and later convicted of fraud, another confessing tearfully on camera, and the word televangelist became a national punch line. The message did not die of embarrassment. It moved into an arena. Joel Osteen inherited his father's Houston congregation in 1999, published Your Best Life Now in 2004, moved the church into a former professional basketball arena in 2005, and preached the gentlest version of the old formula to the largest crowds in the country. Bowler's sharpest observation is the one that cuts closest to home: prosperity is not a fringe. In its soft form, God wants you happy, victorious, and improving, it preaches from respectable stages that would never claim the label. The megachurch laughed at the televangelist and shared his anthropology. We mocked the far end of our own machine.

sections.title: What the Era's Own Instruments Found
sections.body:
Then the era was measured, twice, by its own kind of instrument, the survey, and the findings should be read the way a man reads his own biopsy. In 2005 the sociologist Christian Smith, with Melinda Lundquist Denton, published Soul Searching, drawing on a national study of the religious lives of American teenagers. The teenagers were not hostile to religion. They were content with it, vague about it, and strikingly uniform in it, and what they actually believed, across denominations, Smith summarized in five propositions his team had to invent a name for: a God exists who created the world and watches over life; God wants people to be good, nice, and fair; the central goal of life is to be happy and to feel good about yourself; God is not needed except when a problem needs solving; good people go to heaven. Moralistic Therapeutic Deism, the researchers called it, faith in a god who is, in Smith's words, "a combination Divine Butler and Cosmic Therapist." The finding under the finding was the damning one. The teenagers had not misheard the church. They had heard it perfectly. A half century of preaching that led with a wonderful plan for your life had formed precisely the faith they described, not the faith the churches claimed to teach, and children are the most honest auditors an institution ever gets.

Two years later the flagship audited itself, and, to its lasting credit, published the results. In 2007 Willow Creek released a congregational study called REVEAL, led by its executive pastor Greg Hawkins with Cally Parkinson, and its central finding, by the church's own account, was this: increasing participation in church activities did not correspond to growth in maturity, in love for God and neighbor. The busiest people were not the deepest people. Growth tracked instead with personal practices, Scripture and prayer chief among them, and some of the most spiritually mature people in the building reported the most dissatisfaction with it, and some were considering leaving. Willow's leaders said publicly that the findings were hard to receive, and they changed course, and other churches that ran the same survey found the same pattern in their own pews. Let the weight of that land. The most studied church in America, the one that had run the model with the most sincerity and the most excellence, reported that the model's dashboard had been measuring the wrong thing. Attendance was countable. Formation was not. The era had optimized what it could count, and McGavran's honest instrument, counting as accountability, had become the thing it was meant to prevent, activity mistaken for fruit.

And now the part I cannot write from a safe distance, because there is no safe distance. Every working pastor of my generation was trained inside this era, and I was. Its books were our textbooks. Its conferences were our continuing education. Its assumptions, that the service is the product, that the visitor is the customer, that growth validates method, that the numbers are the fruit, came to us not as arguments to be weighed but as the definition of the job. I learned to read an attendance spreadsheet before I learned to sit with a dying man. I have called an auditorium a sanctuary and an audience a congregation. I have preached, on more Sundays than I care to count, to backs the stage had taught to watch, and I have felt the small lift when the numbers came in high and told myself the lift was joy over the lost. We were not cynics, almost none of us. That is the terrible part. The sincerity was real, the conversions were real, and the machine we served with our sincerity was forming consumers underneath our preaching. Including the preacher.

So let the era have its honest verdict, both halves of it. The attractional model attracted. It filled rooms in a half century when nearly every other Western institution was emptying, it lowered the threshold of the church's door further than any generation had managed, and real people met the living Christ in rented theaters and glass cathedrals, and I will not sneer at a single one of them. What it could not do was form. A crowd gathers around what it already wants. A church is formed into what it does not yet want: repentance, patience, the neighbor, the cross. The era's own instruments returned the verdict, activity without maturity, a generation catechized into a kind god with no demands, an audience standing where a body was supposed to be. By 2010 the machinery still gleamed. And the children raised inside it, the most honestly catechized generation the model ever produced, were quietly heading for the doors. Where they went is the next era's story. The difference between a crowd and a church is the whole question, and it cannot be answered from the stage, because the stage is what asked it. It is answered in the seats, one ordinary Tuesday at a time. The seats were starting to empty.

keyFigures.name: Billy Graham
keyFigures.note: The evangelist whose 1949 Los Angeles crusade taught American Christianity that a crowd could be produced.

keyFigures.name: Donald McGavran
keyFigures.note: Missionary to India whose church growth research, Understanding Church Growth (1970), was carried from the mission field to the suburbs.

keyFigures.name: Robert Schuller
keyFigures.note: Pastor of the drive-in church and the Crystal Cathedral, who built ministry on the unchurched customer's stated needs.

keyFigures.name: Bill Hybels
keyFigures.note: Founder of Willow Creek (1975) and architect of the seeker service, whose church later audited its own model and published the result.

keyFigures.name: Rick Warren
keyFigures.note: Founder of Saddleback (1980), whose Purpose Driven books gave the era its system and its most famous corrective sentence.

keyFigures.name: Oral Roberts
keyFigures.note: Healing evangelist who carried revival onto television and gave the prosperity message its broadcast wing.

keyFigures.name: Christian Smith
keyFigures.note: Sociologist who, with Melinda Lundquist Denton, named Moralistic Therapeutic Deism (2005), the faith the era actually formed.
